speaker: René Redzepi
title: Noma 2.0: No Compromises, With Rene Redzepi
question: In fine dining, why do even fully booked destination restaurants rarely ban guest smartphones the way live comedy shows do?
guest: That would be impossible. People ask me this all the time and I say, "Of course we could. We'd still have guests. We'd still be full." But it is a thing that people just really want and enjoy. And it's almost disrespectful, I think, to people. Funny enough, I was speaking to the team about this the other day, because I remember the first moment that somebody had a smartphone out at Noma and filmed me. And I still remember the feeling of, "Excuse me, you're filming me. You can't do that. You have to ask for permission." And a few weeks passed on and then suddenly it happened again, and again, and again. And now it's just all the time. And so what are you gonna do?

The core reason is that the incentives run in opposite directions. A comedian's product is the material itself: once a set is filmed and posted, the jokes are "spent," punchlines lose their surprise, and half-finished bits can circulate out of context. Recording directly destroys value, so comics like Dave Chappelle and Chris Rock lock phones in Yondr pouches.

A restaurant's product can't be copied by a photo. A picture of a dish transfers none of the taste, service, or atmosphere, so it works as free advertising rather than piracy. Destination restaurants depend heavily on Instagram, social media buzz, and guest-generated images to sustain the global demand that keeps them booked, and many dishes are now designed with photography in mind.

There is also a hospitality problem. Guests paying hundreds of dollars per head expect to be accommodated, not policed, and many want to document a once-in-a-lifetime meal. Confiscating phones feels adversarial, and some diners need to stay reachable over a three-hour tasting menu.

So the few restaurants that do object usually settle for gentle requests, such as no flash or no calls, rather than outright bans.

Unlike stand-up comedy, a restaurant’s core product cannot be stolen by a camera. When a comedian’s set is recorded, leaked clips expose unfinished jokes out of context, spoil punchlines for future ticket buyers, and undercut lucrative streaming specials. By contrast, a photograph of a dish cannot replicate taste, aroma, or pacing; instead of substituting for the experience, guest photos serve as aspirational word-of-mouth that sustains cultural cachet, supports chefs’ broader brands, and keeps future waiting lists full.

Hospitality norms and logistics also work against outright bans. Locking phones in pouches at the door suits a ninety-minute performance in a darkened theater, whereas a tasting menu spans three or four hours and hinges on making guests feel indulged rather than policed. High-paying travelers and celebratory diners expect to stay reachable for babysitters or drivers, look up unfamiliar wine or culinary terms, and document a milestone meal. Confiscating devices or turning servers into floor enforcers introduces adversarial friction that clashes with warm service, so most elite dining rooms simply prohibit flash photography, bright screens, and voice calls.

Mainly because the two businesses depend on phones in opposite ways.

For a comedian, the act itself is what's being sold. A leaked clip can spoil a punchline, expose material that's still being worked out in a club, or let a half-finished joke go viral out of context. Comedy also depends on a shared room, where one glowing screen can break the timing and the laughter.

For a restaurant, a photo can't replace the meal. You can't taste an Instagram post, so pictures of dishes work as free advertising that brings in new bookings. Even top restaurants that are full now need that steady attention to stay in demand, keep winning awards and fill future seats. Dinner is also a private experience at each table rather than a performance for the whole room. A phone mostly distracts its own table, and long meals mean guests may need to check on children, work or the bill.

Hospitality matters too. Taking phones away, for example with the locked pouches some comedy shows use, would feel controlling in a place meant to pamper people. The few chefs who tried photo bans or tight limits mostly got backlash, so most restaurants now just ask guests to be polite: no flash, and calls taken outside.

Live comedy and fine dining face opposite incentives around phones. For comedians, a smartphone threatens the product itself: a leaked clip spoils unreleased jokes across a tour or special, and glowing screens break the shared attention a live room requires. A photo of a plated dish, by contrast, never ruins the experience of tasting it.

In fact, guest photography works in a restaurant’s favor. Even fully booked destination spots rely on ongoing cultural prestige to sustain waitlists, recruit talent, and support cookbooks or sister ventures. Diners posting immaculate plates provide effortless, high-status marketing—and for guests spending hundreds of dollars, documenting the memory and social cachet is often part of what they are buying.

Finally, luxury hospitality prizes warmth and autonomy over crowd control. Locking phones in pouches for a three-hour meal feels adversarial and inconveniences guests who may need to reach family or work, so elite restaurants stick to gentle norms like banning flash photography instead.

A comedy show depends on a whole room paying attention at the same moment. A glowing screen can distract both the performer and the audience, and a clip posted online can spoil a joke the comic plans to tell again tomorrow.

A restaurant has a different bargain with its guests. Someone who has traveled for a special meal may see a quick photo as part of the occasion. If they take it discreetly, the next table can still enjoy the dish, and a shared photo can keep even a fully booked restaurant in the public eye. A blanket ban also puts servers in the awkward position of policing guests they’re there to welcome. Asking diners to skip flash, take calls outside, or put the phone away when it disrupts service usually addresses the problem directly.
